identity.question: Targeted strongest-equivalent scientific review. Read Agterberg-Kaur microscopic Rashba helical stability source, extract exact normal Hamiltonian/helicity DOS convention deltaN and strong-SOC approximation, pairing interaction and Eilenberger/free-energy regularization, coupled finite-wavevector perturbation operator including both fluctuation sectors around a single-q selfconsistent state, and actual helical-to-multiple-q instability boundaries. Compare model assumptions to this compact Zhuang2026 report context: clean 2D isotropic parabolic Rashba gas, strong SOC weak inplane Zeeman field, common singlet single-q pairing, helicity DOS asymmetry alphatilde=.25, quoted weak-to-strong helical critical endpoint TCEP/Tc approximately .05, missing exact hCEP/qCEP. Does your paper already prove or numerically establish that actual endpoint is preempted by stripe/multiple-q order at the same density asymmetry, or merely establish such instability in a different parameter domain? Provide explicit change-of-convention mapping where supported; do not equate generic existence of stripe with actual endpoint preemption. Are quantities sufficient for a source-native finite Gaussian local stability test without fitting phenomenological coefficients? Distinguish negative eigenvalue local instability from global phase selection and from gap closing. Identify exact missing coordinates, dimensions/geometry, angular/frequency grids/cutoffs, published code/data, strongest relevant precedent and limitations. Explain whether any source-specific new consequential finite endpoint inference remains, rather than new solver or known stripe boundary. Use compact equations and source citations; no simulation. Explicitly identify unread external citations and gaps, all source hashes, actual sections inspected.

answers.answer: The paper establishes a finite-wavevector local helical-to-multiple-q instability in its own phase diagrams, but does not establish preemption of the Zhuang2026 endpoint at the same 2D density asymmetry. Its δN>0.25 statement belongs to the reported 3D spherical-Fermi-surface analysis; no matching Zhuang endpoint calculation is given.

answers.answer: The source defines δN=(N+−N−)/(N++N−). Thus αtilde=0.25 maps to δN=0.25 only if αtilde uses the same signed normalized helicity-DOS difference and band ordering; otherwise only the magnitude correspondence is supported. No TCEP, qCEP, fixed-density procedure, or direct Zhuang2026 convention mapping is supplied.

answers.answer: The displayed equations suffice in principle for a source-native finite Gaussian/local stability test: solve the self-consistent single-q state and evaluate the quadratic form in the coupled fluctuation sectors. They do not suffice to reproduce a unique numerical boundary because angular grids, Matsubara truncation/high-frequency treatment, convergence rules, and code/data are unspecified.

references.section: III.B. Stability of the helical phase

answers.answer: A negative eigenvalue of the quadratic fluctuation form is a local instability of the self-consistent helical state. It is not by itself proof of global phase selection and is not equivalent to quasiparticle gap closing; the paper treats free-energy phase comparison and DOS separately.

references.section: III.B. Stability of the helical phase

assumptions: The nontrivial analysis uses an in-plane field; vector potential is neglected and B=H.
findings.claim: The normal Hamiltonian is H0=Σkss′ c†k,s{εkσ0+[αgk+μBH]·σ}ss′ck,s′ plus the pairing interaction, with gk=(ky,−kx,0)/kF and ⟨gk²⟩=1. The helicity dispersions are Ek,±=εk±|αgk+μBH|; in strong SOC the problem reduces to two real helicity bands. For the cylindrical in-plane-field representation, the field can be absorbed into shifted momenta in the quoted dispersion.
limitations: No Zhuang-style αtilde, fixed-density procedure, or exact endpoint convention is defined.

assumptions: The singlet interaction and large-SOC phase redefinition are used.
findings.claim: The pairing interaction is spin-singlet, with V(k̂,k̂′)=−VϕΓ(k̂)ϕΓ*(k̂′) and helicity-band matrix proportional to [[1,−1],[−1,1]]. The factorized gaps obey Δ̃+(R)+Δ̃−(R)=0, so their magnitudes are equal pointwise.
limitations: This is not a general mixed singlet-triplet or independent-helicity-gap model.

references.section: III.C. Density of states in the helical phase

assumptions: The displayed quasiclassical functional is used after solving the Eilenberger equations.
A is neglected for the reported Zeeman-only diagrams.
findings.claim: The Eilenberger equations impose f†f+g²=1; the gap equation sums Matsubara frequencies and helicity bands weighted by Nj; and the Gibbs functional contains V−1|Δ|² minus the Matsubara sum of Ij. No numerical Matsubara cutoff or explicit high-frequency subtraction is stated.
limitations: Angular quadrature, Matsubara truncation, high-frequency treatment, spatial discretization, tolerances, and code/data are absent.

assumptions: The background ΔQ is self-consistent and made real by gauge choice.
Terms through second order in the two added Fourier amplitudes are retained.
findings.claim: The coupled fluctuation sectors are Δp and Δ2Q−p. The required first- and second-order propagator corrections lead to a quadratic free energy with diagonal terms and sector mixing, implying a 2×2 Hermitian local stability matrix.
equations: The paper reports numerically that the first instability occurs at p=−Q.
limitations: Full coefficient functions, eigenvectors, numerical grids, and error estimates are not printed.
The determinant/eigenvalue criterion is inferred from the displayed quadratic form.

findings.claim: For isotropic s-wave pairing on a 3D spherical Fermi surface, δN=0 has helical-to-multiple-q instability below T/Tc=0.36; δN=0.05 retains a low-temperature/moderate-field multiple-q region; and the stripe region shrinks with δN, ceasing once δN>0.25. A separate 2D cylindrical result is discussed for Hc2, but no 2D isotropic-s-wave helical-to-multiple-q endpoint boundary at δN=0.25 is supplied.
equations: δN=0.05: multiple-q at low temperature and moderate fields.
